food.text: During the Neolithic, Anatolia was an early center for the development of farming, which originated in the adjacent Fertile Crescent. Around 9,000 years ago, Anatolian Neolithic farmers migrated into Europe, and their descendants came to dominate the continent as far west as the Iberian Peninsula and the British Isles.

Çatalhöyük was a very large proto-city settlement on the Konya Plain in southern Anatolia, existing from around 7500 BC to 5600 BC and flourishing around 7000 BC. The people there cultivated a variety of domesticated wheat species, and the different varieties of crop bolstered food supplies against crop failure.

The people of Çatalhöyük grew peas and harvested almonds, pistachios and fruit from trees in the surrounding hills. Bread and porridge were prepared, and remains of dome ovens are present at early layers of the site.
At Çatalhöyük, hunting remained a major source of food alongside domestication. The community ate fish, birds, and smaller mammals like foxes and hares.

Çayönü in eastern Anatolia is regarded as the oldest of the major Neolithic settlements, dated to about 7250 to 6750 BC. Its town had a central square with buildings of stone and mud, and finds include farming tools suggesting both crops and animal husbandry, as well as the domestication of the dog.

Proteins recovered on ceramic remains show that dairy products like cow milk were consumed at the Western Mound of Çatalhöyük. Remains of cattle and sheep at the site, with evidence of animal penning and dung, indicate some degree of domestication or management of these animals.

art.text: The most elaborate Neolithic wall paintings in the Near East are found at Çatal Höyük in Central Anatolia. They date to about 7000 to 6500 BC.

Çayönü in eastern Anatolia is regarded as the oldest of the early Neolithic towns, dated to about 7250 to 6750 BC. Its layout is well understood: buildings of stone and mud were arranged around a central square.

Religion at Çayönü, one of Anatolia's earliest Neolithic settlements, is represented by figurines of Cybele, the mother goddess. These small sculptures are among the region's earliest artistic expressions of belief.
Inside homes at Çatal Höyük, mural compositions depict complex scenes combining humans and animals, including bulls and deer. These scenes are often interpreted as hunting scenes or ritual dances.

The Urfa Man, found at a site near Göbekli Tepe, dates to the Pre-Pottery Neolithic period circa 9000 BC. It is considered the oldest naturalistic life-sized sculpture of a human. Slightly later, stone and fired clay human statuettes appeared at Mureybet, dated to 8500 to 8000 BC.

The Chalcolithic era in Anatolia, about 5500 to 3000 BC, is defined by the first metal implements made with copper. It is represented by sites such as Hacilar, Beycesultan, Mersin Yumuktepe and Norşuntepe.

war.text: The Kura-Araxes culture, whose earliest evidence is on the Ararat plain in the Armenian highlands around 4000 BC, produced weapons including arrows, daggers, battle axes and spears made from obsidian, flint, bone and bronze. These weapons were found at sites of the Shengavit civilization such as Shengavit itself, in the present-day Yerevan area.

The Maykop culture of the western Caucasus, dated to about 3700 to 3000 BC, produced weapons such as tanged daggers and single-bladed cast shaft hole axes made using two-sided molds. This metalworking, along with the use of arsenical copper, was later borrowed by the Yamnaya culture of the steppes.

Around 3000 BC, in the transitional EBI-EBII period, the previous significant Uruk-oriented settlement at Arslantepe was hit by widespread burning and destruction. The article describes the level as destroyed in a violent conflagration. After this, pottery of the Kura-Araxes culture, a mainly pastoralist people connected with the Caucasus mountains, appeared in the area.

Excavations at Arslantepe uncovered weapons 45 to 60 centimeters long, long enough to be described as short swords or long daggers, along with 12 spearheads. These finds belong to level VI A, dated to about 3400 to 3200 BC.

Stone and clay molds for casting weapons were found at Shengavit and Margahovit, sites of the Kura-Araxes culture near Yerevan. Together with finds of arsenical bronze near Yerevan, they show that weapons and tools were being produced locally by this culture.

Phase VI A at Arslantepe, the level that produced the short swords, daggers and spearheads, ended in destruction when the city was burned. The article says Arslantepe was violently destroyed at the end of this phase (Late Chalcolithic 5), leaving a number of small finds in place where they lay. Unlike other Uruk expansion settlements, which were abandoned and stripped of anything of note, Arslantepe was not emptied before it fell.

science.text: Ancient DNA has shown that agriculture reached Europe largely through migration, not just the spread of ideas. Before this, the lack of ancient human DNA from pre-Neolithic times meant it was unknown how the spread had happened. Archaeology alone had long shown that farming moved from the Middle East to Europe.

The earliest farmers in Anatolia derived most of their ancestry from the region's local hunter-gatherers. This suggests that local hunter-gatherers adopted agriculture themselves rather than having it spread into the region by demic diffusion.

A 2025 study found that the spread of Neolithic cultures in Western Anatolia and the Aegean was complex. It involved admixture between Central Anatolian farmers and Western Anatolian hunter-gatherers who adopted farming. The classic Anatolian Farmer genetic profile formed sometime after 7000 BC, and adoption of agriculture involved cultural exchange rather than pure migration.

Çayönü Tepe, a typical Pre-Pottery Neolithic B site, may be where some of the first animal domestication occurred. The pig may have first been domesticated there in 8,500 BCE. Earliest dates for domestication elsewhere in northern Mesopotamia are c. 9000 BCE for goats and sheep and c. 8000 BCE for cattle.

The Kura-Araxes culture, an early Bronze Age culture assigned to c. 4000 to 2200 BC, has its earliest evidence on the Ararat plain. From there it spread to Georgia by 3000 BC, though it never reached Colchis. It also moved south-east into an area below the Urmia basin and Lake Van.

Volcanic obsidian from the island of Milos was used to make tools and weapons from the Mesolithic to the late Neolithic. It traveled widely, reaching mainland Greece and Western Anatolia, and possibly as far as Egypt. Groups apparently landed intermittently to collect stone, since there is no evidence of settlements on Milos until the Final Neolithic (4000 BC).

The use of clay plaster for floor and wall coverings during the Pre-Pottery Neolithic B is believed to have led to the discovery of pottery. The earliest proto-pottery was White Ware vessels, made from lime and gray ash and built up around baskets before firing, around 7000 BC. The PPNB culture may also have had northerly origins, possibly from northeastern Anatolia.

politics.text: In Armenia's Late Chalcolithic Areni and Godedzor traditions, dated to about 4,300 to 3,500 BC, societies grew increasingly complex. They developed centralized hierarchies and status symbols such as scepters and stamp seals, alongside prestige goods of gold, silver, and lapis lazuli.

The Leyla-Tepe culture of the South Caucasus, dated from about 3800 to 3200 BC, built the Soyugbulag kurgans in what is now Kaspi Municipality, central Georgia. These burial mounds date to the beginning of the 4th millennium BC, an unexpectedly early appearance of such elite monuments in the region.

By 3000 BC, the Kura-Araxes culture had spread from the Armenian highlands north into the Caucasus. It came to cover a vast area about 1,000 km by 500 km, reaching eastern Georgia, Azerbaijan, eastern Turkey, and as far as northern Iraq.

These same communities also began building kurgans and burying their dead in large jars, marking the rise of local elites in southern Armenia. Such practices, along with the era's first rudiments of monumental architecture, reflected societies moving toward more centralized power structures.

According to archaeologist Geoffrey Summers, Kura-Araxes peoples suddenly moved into Iran and the Van region shortly before 3000 BC. He linked this migration to the 'Late Uruk Collapse', the sudden end of the Uruk period around 3100 BC.

Artifacts from the Leyla-Tepe culture closely resemble objects excavated at the ancient city of Tel Khazneh I in Syria, both dating from the 4th millennium BC. This similarity, identified by a Russian Academy of Sciences expedition, points to far-reaching contacts across the ancient Near East.

Some researchers have credited the Leyla-Tepe culture's early copper metallurgy to migrants from Uruk in Mesopotamia arriving around 4500 BC. Others instead point to earlier pre-Uruk traditions, such as the late Ubaid period, as the source of its development.

culture.text: Around 5900 BC, villagers at Gadachrili tried to divert the Shulaveri river into nearby fields using a system of canals. This is the oldest example of water management in the Caucasus. The attempt seems to have worked, though sediment probably meant the canals needed regular maintenance.

The Shulaveri–Shomu people were proficient farmers whose livelihood rested on cereal cultivation and animal breeding. Their sites hold goat, sheep, cow, pig and dog from the earliest phase. Crops included 10 species of wheat, several types of barley, cultivated grape and melon.

Çatalhöyük in central Turkey, dated to about 7,000 BCE, is considered the most advanced of Anatolia's Neolithic settlements. Others in the list include Çayönü, Nevali Cori, Aşıklı Höyük, Hacilar and Göbekli Tepe. Together they show Anatolia was an early center for farming.

The Kura–Araxes culture existed from about 4000 BC until about 2000 BC, and its earliest evidence is on the Ararat plain in the Armenian highlands. It spread north into the Caucasus by 3000 BC. At its height it covered an area about 1,000 km by 500 km.

Çayönü in eastern Anatolia is considered the oldest of the region's major Neolithic towns, dated to c. 7250–6750 BC. Its town layout was built around a central square, with buildings of stone and mud. Finds include farming tools and evidence of dog domestication.
Shengavit Settlement in the present-day Yerevan area of Armenia was inhabited from about 3200 BC cal to 2500 BC cal. The town covered six hectares, which is large for a Kura–Araxes site.
Bronze metallurgy spread to Anatolia from the Transcaucasian Kura-Araxes culture in the late 4th millennium BCE. This marked the beginning of the Bronze Age in the region.
Religion at Çayönü is represented by figurines of Cybele, the mother goddess. Hacilar in western Turkey followed Çayönü and has been dated to 7040 BC.

After 3000 BC, metal objects became much more common at Kura–Araxes sites. Copper objects with an arsenical component of up to 25% took on a shiny greyish, silvery colour. It is quite possible these high arsenical alloys were meant to imitate silver.

At Çatalhöyük, a stately goddess seated on a throne flanked by two lionesses was found in a grain bin. Its excavator Mellaart suggested it might have been a means of ensuring the harvest or protecting the food supply.
The rich tomb of a woman at Kvazchela is a good example of the growing metalwork of the Kura–Araxes culture. It is quite similar to the 'royal tomb' from Arslantepe.
